title: Fuzz's Fluffy Stand
markdown:
In Aeridor, stone towers tickled clouds and emerald valleys draped like scarves. Wind-swept ridges, whispering pines. Nerin belonged there as much as the air. He moved with a hawk’s grace; eyes sharp as mountain weather noticed everything. His humour was dry as a desert pebble, and he often chuckled when no one else quite understood.

His dearest friend was Willow the hare, nose twitching with a thousand thoughts a minute, paws ready to thump encouragement. And Fuzz: Nerin’s familiar, a cloud-puff the colour of summer sky, usually soft as a sigh. Fuzz loved Nerin the way only mist and affection can.

The Annual Village Blossom Contest. Finest floral arrangements, fragrant herbs, dazzling dewdrop sculptures. Nerin’s task: a single perfect mountain bloom, guided into place by Fuzz, a gentle puff, not a petal out of line. Delicate control. His specialty.

“Now, Fuzz.” A star-shaped Wind Whisper in his hands. “A gentle puff. A whisper of air.”

Fuzz, usually obliging, remained stubbornly still. A mountain of fluffy conviction. Nerin nudged with an elbow. Nothing. A coaxing word. Still nothing. Willow tapped a foot. “Perhaps it’s having a moment.”

Nerin’s stomach fluttered. Not the moment for a fluffy monument. The contest would begin. If Fuzz did not cooperate, the entry would wilt. Sun dipping, long shadows, his turn coming sooner than he liked. A sigh that tasted of worry. He liked things smooth, a well-tuned harp. This was not that.

The contest began with a rustle of programmes and a judge clearing a throat that had opinions. Elara Meadowlight’s dewdrop fountain shimmered into tiny rainbows and made a child clap without meaning to. Osric Boulderhand’s pet rock, painted with glow-moss, pulsed a gentle steady light and looked, Nerin thought, quietly pleased to have been invited. The square a riot of colour and scent: crushed petals, honey, someone’s overambitious garlic wreath. Nerin to the side with a perfectly still bloom and a stubbornly unmoving cloud. He fiddled a loose thread. Stressed pine smelled sharper. The crowd’s murmur felt like judgment. Fingers clumsy on the tunic.

“That dragon is trying to be subtle,” Willow whispered, ears toward Master Grok’s entry: an enormous grumpy dragon carved from a single pine log, painted eyes glaring, mossy scales rough. “Not its strongest subject. That much wood is very heavy.”

Nerin’s heart sank a little. He was supposed to present with effortless charm, no fuss. Trying too hard was not his style, and Fuzz was forcing him into exactly that awkwardness. Goblin Nibs ambled over, brow furrowed, weaver of finest silks, nimble fingers, kind heart, patched tunic smelling of woodsmoke and good sense. “Having trouble? Fuzz looks rather resolute. As if it’s decided to become part of the mountain.”

“It appears Fuzz has decided to take root.” Dry as ever; eyes worried. Nibs offered a tiny daisy chain of spun moonlight. “Perhaps this will tickle its fancy.” Nerin tied it around a fluffy swirl that was not quite a neck. Fuzz wobbled, a little puff, then settled, the chain lost in vast fluff.

Nerin’s gaze drifted to moonpetal flowers, each with its own inner light. An unwelcome thought: Willow could nudge the bloom with a hind leg; another elf might lend a puff. He took a step, caught himself. Shame tightened. Giving in felt like a failure of plan and quiet strength. Fuzz, despite stubbornness, radiated unshakeable purpose. This was Fuzz’s moment too, even if the moment was immense immovability.

A small gust swept the square, the kind that thinks it is helpful. It ruffled Elara’s fountain into a brief extra rainbow and sent Osric’s pet rock tumbling with a gentle clatter onto soft grass, where it continued to glow, unbothered. Not a disaster. A disruption. Fuzz’s stillness looked more deliberate, a punctuation mark the wind could not edit. Stakes higher. His turn soon. Willow’s ears said, without words, that a hare could shove a flower if asked, and that she hoped she would not be asked.

He looked at Fuzz, then the Wind Whisper. A strange calm, quiet before rain. He would not fight. He would give up the perfect plan, the need for control, the fear of seeming ruffled, and trust the fluffy enigma. “Willow. Fine shimmering moss from the shadowed glen. Damp earth and old secrets. Cool and soft.”

Willow’s ears flicked; she was off, white tail a blur. Nerin breathed pine and wildflowers. He plucked wisps, cool, damp, alive, ancient. He placed the bloom not on Fuzz but beside it, anchoring it in moss, a miniature landscape spilling to the ground.

When his turn came he walked to the centre, fluid, confident, as if the harp inside him had found its pitch without Fuzz’s puff. He did not coax. He gestured. “The essence of Aeridor. The unyielding spirit of the mountains.” Fuzz, who declined to bow. “And this is the steadfast heart. It does not move. It simply is.”

A judge wrote something. A child whispered that the cloud had won already. Moss and bloom, earthy scent meeting the Wind Whisper’s perfume. Fuzz, a faint tremor, puffed a little more, a contented sigh that was not the puff Nerin had asked for and was better. The bloom in dark damp moss, unmoving Fuzz as guardian, looked not incomplete but like a statement of quiet strength. Judges murmured, eyes travelling from petal to puff and back.

Then, in its magnificent stillness, Fuzz began to release tiny shimmering motes—not a puff, a slow exhalation of soft luminescence, fairy dust, illuminating the petals as if moonlight had been asked politely. More beautiful than any fussy arrangement. The crowd gasped, then admired. Fuzz, by refusing to puff, had made a light.

Nerin’s quiet pride. He had not tried too hard; he had listened. Willow thumped a triumphant rhythm. Nibs beamed. Fuzz gave a contented shimmer, stubbornness satisfied. Osric retrieved his rock and, to his credit, nodded at a cloud that would not be rushed. Nerin, dry wit softened, stood with Fuzz as they were: a winning combination, whether or not anyone kept score.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
